Homer, Hesiod, Pindar and others called Neptune γαιήοχον [earth-holding] or γεήοχον [earth-holding]: some grammarians believed this name to mean γαῖαν ἔχοντα [holding the earth], others γαῖαν ὀχοῦντα [carrying the earth], some γαίοντα [rejoicing] ὄχοις [in chariots], which is not likely to have occurred to any of the ancients, so that it was defended in vain by Doederlein in his Homeric Glossary and by Nitzsch in Philologus vol. 3 p. 10. Add to this that γαιάοχος [earth-holding] is also an epithet of other deities who have nothing to do with chariots: so it is incredible that the poets used γαιήοχον [earth-holding] in such a way that it would have to be derived sometimes from γαîα [earth], sometimes from γαίειν [to rejoice]. Therefore, comparing what has been said about this epithet in Thes. vol. 1, 2 p. 2315 and vol. 2 p. 490 (where Ἐρεχθέος γαιηόχου [of Erechtheus the earth-holder] is to be added from an inscription found by Ross on the acropolis), there is no doubt that γαιάοχος [earth-holding] is ὁ γαῖαν ἔχων [the one holding the earth].
